article.overview: An ion spectrometer is an instrument that identifies electrically charged atoms and molecules (ions) by measuring their energy, their mass-to-charge ratio, or both. On the Moon, ion spectrometers have been used to study solar-wind ions striking the surface, ions released from the surface and exosphere, and the plasma environment around the Moon. Because 'ion spectrometer' describes a measurement technique rather than one standard design, this article compares three flown examples: the Apollo Suprathermal Ion Detector Experiment (SIDE), the Kaguya MAP-PACE Ion Mass Analyzer (IMA) and the Chang'e-6 Negative Ions at the Lunar Surface (NILS) instrument.
article.description:
An ion spectrometer collects charged particles arriving from a defined direction, sorts them by energy per charge and, in many designs, by mass per charge, and records how many ions arrive in each channel. The resulting spectrum allows scientists to infer which ion species are present and what plasma or surface processes produced them.

The Moon has no substantial atmosphere, so the ions it hosts are produced in several ways. Solar-wind protons and other particles strike the surface and are partly reflected or sputtered, ultraviolet light ionises the thin exosphere, and the Moon passes through the magnetotail and magnetosheath of the Earth, where ion populations differ from the solar wind [1][4]. Ion spectrometers measure these populations directly, which is why they are complementary to magnetometers and electric-field instruments.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
Ion spectrometers on the Moon address three broad questions: which ions are present at and above the surface, how solar-wind plasma interacts with the surface and with crustal magnetic fields, and how the surface charges electrically in the plasma environment.

The Apollo SIDE was designed to measure energy and mass spectra of positive ions close to the lunar surface, to measure ion flux and energy spectra in Earth's magnetotail and magnetosheath when the Moon passed through them, to study the plasma interaction between the solar wind and the Moon, and to determine a preliminary value for the lunar surface electric potential [1]. The Kaguya IMA adds ion mass identification to the energy measurements of its companion ion energy analyser, and it observes ions leaving the lunar surface [3][5]. NILS was designed to detect negative ions produced when solar-wind particles strike the surface; these ions are short-lived and cannot reach orbit, so the instrument had to operate near the surface [6][8].
article.operating_principle:
An ion spectrometer typically admits ions through an aperture, selects them by energy per charge with an electrostatic analyser, and then separates them by mass using a velocity (Wien) filter or a time-of-flight measurement.

The Apollo SIDE Mass Analyzer combined a Wien velocity filter, a curved-plate electrostatic energy-per-charge filter and a channel electron multiplier operated as an ion counter. It measured ion flux in 20 mass channels across six energy levels [1]. The SIDE Total Ion Detector had no velocity filter; it used a channel electron multiplier to detect higher-energy ions in 20 energy steps [1].

The Kaguya IMA is described in the cited literature as a time-of-flight energy-mass spectrometer that identifies ion species by their mass [4]. Its published mass resolution is about M/dM of 20 in a 2009 conference abstract [4].

The NILS instrument combines a compact electrostatic analyser with a time-of-flight cell to measure energy per charge and mass per charge of incident ions. It views one direction at a time, so electrostatic scanning is needed to change its look direction. An electromagnetic electron-suppression system allows switching between negative-ion and electron measurements [9].
article.scientific_importance: Ion measurements complement magnetic-field, electric-field and bulk-plasma observations by showing which ions are present near the surface and how they arrive there. Historical accounts describe the Apollo SIDE as the first instrument package to perform in-situ measurements of ions incident on the lunar surface, although this description was taken from a secondary search summary and should be checked against the original Apollo reports [2]. Kaguya's IMA reported the first direct detection of ions originating from the Moon at about 100 km altitude, including He+, C+, O+, Na+ and K+, which supported the idea of helium, carbon and oxygen exospheres around the Moon [4]. NILS provided the first ESA measurement of negative ions on the lunar surface, a result that could be obtained only by an instrument operating at the surface because the ions are short-lived [6][8].

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal mass, size or power for an ion spectrometer. The three examples below are flown instruments with different sensor designs, mission roles and levels of published engineering detail.

examples.name: Apollo Suprathermal Ion Detector Experiment (SIDE)
examples.type: Historical lunar surface instrument (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package)
examples.sensor_configuration: Mass Analyzer (Wien velocity filter, curved-plate electrostatic energy-per-charge filter, channel electron multiplier operated as ion counter) and Total Ion Detector (channel electron multiplier, no velocity filter).
examples.mass_analyzer_calibration_note: Only the two highest energy levels were well calibrated in the laboratory.
examples.deployment: Placed on the surface by astronauts during the first EVA, levelled with a bubble level, on tripod legs tilted 26 degrees towards the equator, detectors looking upward; ribbon cable to ALSEP central station; wire ground screen to compensate for surface potential.
examples.operating_period_note: Apollo 15 unit turned on around 19:00 UT on 31 July 1972 and commanded off on 12 March 1977; cycled on and off to keep internal temperatures below about 55 degrees C.
examples.qualification: Mass, dimensions and power not stated in the accessed source. Other Apollo SIDE units (Apollo 12 and 14 per search summaries) were not opened in full.

examples.name: Kaguya MAP-PACE Ion Mass Analyzer (IMA)
examples.sensor_configuration: MAP-PACE has four sensors: two electron analysers (ESA-S1, ESA-S2), an ion energy analyser (IEA) with a stated energy limit of less than 28 keV/q, and the ion mass analyser (IMA).
examples.ima_function: Adds ion mass identification to the functions of the IEA; observes ions flying from the lunar surface.
examples.ima_technique_note: Described in the cited literature as a time-of-flight energy-mass spectrometer.
examples.mission: Launched from Tanegashima in September 2007; ended by impacting the Moon on 11 June 2009 per JAXA (a search summary gives 10 June 2009).

examples.name: Chang'e-6 Negative Ions at the Lunar Surface (NILS) instrument
examples.type: Lunar surface instrument (Chang'e-6 lander, ESA-funded, IRF-built)
examples.sensor_configuration: Compact electrostatic analyser combined with a time-of-flight cell; electrostatic elevation scanning; electromagnetic electron suppression to switch between negative-ion and electron measurements.
examples.measurement_target: Negative ions produced when solar-wind particles strike the lunar surface.
examples.operations: Activated about four hours after touchdown; first data collection began 280 minutes after landing; first collection period 23 minutes; intermittent operation; switched off on 3 June 2024 at 15:20 BST; over three hours of data collected.
examples.thermal_note: A conference abstract summarised in search results reports that operators alternated short full-power bursts with long cooling periods because the instrument heated up; not opened in full.
examples.landing: Chang'e-6 landed 1 June 2024 (23:23 BST) in the South Pole-Aitken Basin on the lunar far side.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Not publicly specified for any of the three examples in the sources accessed for this rerun. The Apollo 15 SIDE description gives only the height of the top of the instrument above the surface (about 45 cm). Dimensions of a new instrument would be set by its sensor design, field-of-view and mounting requirements.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Not publicly specified for any of the three examples in the sources accessed for this rerun. Mass determines launch and lander accommodation for any new design; no mass value is estimated here.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified for any of the three examples in the sources accessed for this rerun. Thermal duty-cycling is documented for the Apollo 15 SIDE (temperatures kept below about 55 degrees C) and is described in a search summary for NILS.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
An ion spectrometer on the lunar surface or in lunar orbit must operate in a vacuum with large temperature variations, cosmic and solar radiation, and a plasma environment that can be perturbed by the spacecraft or the surface itself. For surface instruments, the surface electric potential matters because it can alter the energies at which ions reach the sensor; the Apollo SIDE used a ground screen to compensate for this effect [1].

Thermal management is a recurring constraint. The Apollo 15 SIDE was cycled on and off to keep internal temperatures below about 55 degrees C [1]. A conference abstract summarised in the search results reports that NILS operators alternated short full-power bursts with long cooling periods because the instrument heated up; that abstract was not opened in full. Sensors that measure incoming ions also need a clear field of view, so their mounting and orientation matter. NILS, which measures ions that are short-lived near the surface, needed to operate close to the surface to make its measurements [6][8].
article.limitations: A single ion spectrometer measures the ions reaching its aperture from its field of view. It cannot by itself map the global plasma or determine the origin of every ion. The SIDE Mass Analyzer's lowest-energy channels were not well calibrated in the laboratory [1]. Surface potentials and nearby spacecraft or instrument fields can change which ions reach the sensor. NILS views one direction at a time and operated intermittently for about two days, so its data cover a limited set of conditions [6][9]. Mass resolution, energy range and sensitivity cannot be compared across the three examples because each was designed for a different measurement goal and some values are not published.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The three examples illustrate different delivery pathways, and none of them can be treated as a template for a new instrument.
transportation_process: Surface payloads: the Apollo SIDE was delivered to the surface as part of the ALSEP package and deployed by astronauts during an extravehicular activity, with a cable to the ALSEP central station [1].

Surface payloads: NILS was integrated on the Chang'e-6 lander and activated after landing [6]; the deployment mechanism, power and data interfaces and thermal interface are not described in the sources accessed.

Orbiter payloads: MAP-PACE was carried on the KAGUYA orbiter, launched from Tanegashima in September 2007 and operated until its lunar impact in 2009 [3]; orbit insertion, commissioning, pointing and thermal interfaces are not described in the sources accessed.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo SIDE: astronaut placement and levelling on tripod legs during an EVA [1]. NILS: deployment method not publicly specified in the sources accessed. MAP-PACE: orbiter-mounted; not applicable as a surface deployment.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo SIDE was flown on the Apollo ALSEP packages; the Kaguya MAP-PACE IMA flew on an orbiter; NILS flew on the Chang'e-6 lander.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility is asserted between any ion spectrometer and a named lander, rover or spacecraft. Compatibility would depend on verified mass, dimensions, mounting interfaces, landing loads, power, data and thermal requirements for the specific vehicle.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo SIDE contributed to the Apollo lunar surface experiments, which provided some of the first in-situ measurements of lunar surface ions and plasma interaction [1][2]. The Kaguya MAP-PACE IMA provided the first direct detection of ions originating from the Moon, and it supported the idea of an exosphere containing helium, carbon and oxygen [4][5]. NILS was the first ESA instrument on the lunar surface and the first ESA detection of negative ions on the Moon's surface [6][7][8].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
The name 'ion spectrometer' describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design. The Apollo SIDE, Kaguya IMA and NILS examples differ in mission era, sensor architecture, view geometry and published engineering detail, so their values are not interchangeable. Mass, dimensions and power are not publicly specified in the sources accessed for any of the three examples. The Kaguya IMA mass and energy ranges are not stated in the accessed JAXA page. Several technical claims rely on conference abstracts or search summaries that were not opened in full, and these are identified in the text. The article's engineering discussion describes general considerations and is not a design specification for a new ion spectrometer.

Specific evidence gaps for this rerun: the Wieser et al. (2025) NILS paper and the Saito et al. (2010) MAP-PACE paper are behind publisher sign-in pages and were not read in full; the Apollo SIDE final engineering report on NTRS was too large to read in the accessed fetch, so SIDE mass, dimensions and power remain unverified; the KAGUYA impact date differs between sources (11 June 2009 on the JAXA page, 10 June 2009 in a search summary); no verified direct image asset for SIDE hardware was located; the NILS ion-species result is summarised from search results as negative hydrogen ions and should be confirmed in the primary paper.

data_quality_notes: Rerun (v2) of payload 120. The v1 files ion_spectrometer_payload_120.md and .json were not modified.
Category and name taken from lunar_payloads_catalogue_320.md: category 6 'Radiation and space environment', payload 120 'Ion spectrometer'.

The 'ion spectrometer' payload is a class rather than one design; three flown examples were chosen (Apollo SIDE, Kaguya MAP-PACE IMA, Chang'e-6 NILS). Other ion instruments, such as Chandrayaan-3 RAMBHA-LP (a Langmuir probe) and Lunar Vertex MAPS (a plasma spectrometer), were not included.
Mass, dimensions and power are not publicly specified in the accessed sources for any example; values are null rather than estimated.
Primary papers for NILS (Wieser et al. 2025) and MAP-PACE (Saito et al. 2010) were behind sign-in pages; claims citing them rely on search summaries and are flagged in the article.
The Apollo SIDE NTRS final report (19700004894) was too large for the accessed fetch; SIDE specifications rest on the PDS Apollo 15 instrument description and search summaries.
Date discrepancy: KAGUYA impact on 11 June 2009 (JAXA page) versus 10 June 2009 (search summary). JAXA date used.
No verified direct image asset was found for Apollo SIDE hardware; no SIDE image included rather than a null-URL image, which the validator cannot place.
